recall.question: How do shells map to items, and what checks the depth gate?
recall.answer: Shells 0-1 live in items 1-2, shells 2-3 in items 3-6, shell 4 in item 7, shell 5 in item 8, shell 6 in item 9, shell 7 in item 11, shell 8 in item 10, shell 9 in item 12, shell 10 in item 13(c). Item 13 checks the depth gate.

keyTerms.definition: The effective branching factor. The model is as confused as if choosing uniformly among that many tokens.
Memorization wearing an eval costume. Exact-match overlap and canaries detect it.
Loss times tokens over bytes over ln 2. The tokenizer-independent common denominator.
Judge agreement corrected for chance. It asks how much better than coin-flipping the base rate.
The bridge from benchmark lab to deployment field: same inputs, format, and success criterion.
The noise ruler from seed variation. Differences smaller than the band are not differences.

recall.question: Why compare models in bits per byte instead of per-token loss?
recall.answer: Per-token loss divides by the tokenizer's own token count. Bits per byte divides by bytes, which no tokenizer controls.

recall.question: What is the difference between internal and external evals?
recall.answer: Internal evals steer: fast, frequent, inspectable. External evals judge: held-out, versioned, run by someone else. Mixing them inflates the headline.

recall.question: Why do slice tables need confidence intervals?
recall.answer: Slices are small n, small n means wide bands. The table with intervals is the honest report; without them it is a trap.
